action_criteria.label: Brain MRI for ventricular size, iNPH supportive features and an obstructing cause
action_criteria.rationale: Her internist's CT reported enlarged ventricles, so an MRI must measure them, show the supportive features and exclude an obstruction before CSF is removed.

action_criteria.rationale: Her word-finding and calculation complaints make thyroid, B12 and calcium worth checking, but they do not decide the iNPH question.

action_criteria.rationale: A two-year slowing of gait with freezing and a fall needs an objective baseline so that the post-tap change can be measured.

action_criteria.rationale: She misplaces objects and repeats herself, so a MoCA documents whether the profile is dysexecutive or amnestic and sets the baseline for the tap.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Opening pressure 12 cmH2O, normal cells, protein and glucose; 40 mL removed; TUG 27 to 20 s at 2 hours and 18 s at 24 hours (33%), 10-metre walk 20 to 14 s, MoCA 21 to 24
action_criteria.label: Lumbar tap test with opening pressure and CSF removal
action_criteria.rationale: Normal-pressure CSF and an objective response to removing 30 to 50 mL make iNPH probable and predict shunt benefit.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TUG 20 s at 2 hours and 18 s at 24 hours (33% faster); 10-metre walk 14 s at 24 hours (30% faster); no freezing; MoCA 24/30
action_criteria.label: Post-tap timed gait reassessment
action_criteria.rationale: Repeating the same timed measures at 2 and 24 hours after the tap turns her response into numbers that can be compared with the baseline.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform the large-volume lumbar tap before brain MRI has excluded a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not attribute the syndrome to normal ageing or deconditioning once the ventriculomegaly and the tap response are documented
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 33% in TUG at 24 hours, the DESH MRI (Evans index 0.39, callosal angle 71 degrees) and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]

Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) and continued osteoporosis treatment (alendronate, calcium and vitamin D) while awaiting surgery, given a fall with a wrist injury and her fracture risk

avoided_actions.rationale: She has had no episodes suggesting seizures, so an EEG cannot help separate iNPH from its mimics.
Her only fall was a trip on uneven pavement without loss of consciousness, so an ECG does not inform the gait work-up.
There is no syncope, murmur or embolic event, so echocardiography has no role in this work-up.
She had a head CT three weeks ago; MRI measures the callosal angle, temporal horns and aqueduct better and is available.
The fall was mechanical, not syncopal, so rhythm monitoring has no diagnostic role here.
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are
A two-year afebrile gait syndrome with normal-pressure CSF and one white cell gives no indication for prion, inflammatory or infectious assays.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Only thin Fazekas 1 periventricular caps with no deep lesions, far less than the ventriculomegaly, and the gait improves after the tap.
Freezing and reduced arm swing overlap, but there is no rest tremor, rigidity or asymmetry, vertical gaze is full, and the gait responds to CSF removal.
Free recall improves with cues within a dysexecutive profile, naming is preserved, the hippocampi are MTA 1, and gait and urgency led the syndrome despite her mother's late-life memory problems.

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Ventricles are enlarged out of proportion to the sulci, with DESH and a callosal angle of 71 degrees, and the gait improves after the tap.

differential.diagnosis: Secondary communicating hydrocephalus (post-traumatic, post-haemorrhagic or post-meningitic)
differential.key_features: No head injury, subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis in the history.

key_clinical_evidence: Probable iNPH needs an insidious gait disturbance after age 40 lasting at least 3 to 6 months with cognitive or urinary symptoms, no antecedent cause, ventriculomegaly (Evans index greater than 0.3) not explained by atrophy, and a CSF opening pressure of 5 to 18 mmHg (7 to 24.5 cmH2O) [Relkin_2005].
DESH and an acute callosal angle support the diagnosis; here Evans 0.39, DESH and a callosal angle of 71 degrees [Nakajima_2021].

The tap test removes 30 to 50 mL and repeats the timed gait measures at 2 to 4 and 24 hours [Nakajima_2021]; a 10% or greater TUG improvement is a commonly used positive threshold, though no guideline sets a single cut-off. Its sensitivity is 26% to 61% and its PPV 73% to 100%, so a single negative tap does not exclude shunt-responsive iNPH [Marmarou_2005].
With osteoporosis and one injurious fall already, the falls risk of the iNPH gait carries a high fracture risk while she awaits surgery.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Late-life memory problems of unknown cause in one parent do not explain a gait-led syndrome with a dysexecutive profile, cue-responsive recall and MTA 1 hippocampi that improves after CSF removal.
red_herrings.data_point: Mother had memory problems in 80s, etiology unknown
red_herrings.intended_effect: The cognitive decline is attributed to familial Alzheimer's disease

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]
The timed gait is repeated after the tap, at 2 to 24 hours, so that its change from the baseline measures the response to CSF removal [Nakajima_2021]

metadata.difficulty_variant_description: Straightforward iNPH in a 74-year-old left-handed retired pharmacist: gait, cognitive and urinary symptoms, Evans index 0.39 with DESH and a callosal angle of 71 degrees, and a tap response (TUG 33% faster at 24 hours); a maternal history of late-life memory problems as a minor red herring, and osteoporosis raising the stakes of her falls.

patient.chief_complaint: Difficulty walking, urinary leakage and memory decline over the past two years; brought in by her family for evaluation

family_history: Mother had memory problems in 80s, etiology unknown

social_history.living_situation: Lives with husband; son visits weekly

patient.history_present_illness: A 74-year-old left-handed retired pharmacist with hypertension and osteoporosis was admitted for evaluation of a two-year progressive decline in gait, bladder control and memory. Her husband, a retired engineer, has kept meticulous notes of her functional decline and brought them to the admission. He documents the onset approximately two years ago, when she began walking more slowly and taking smaller steps. She fell once on uneven pavement nine months ago and sustained a right wrist contusion; she has used a cane since then. She describes her legs as 'not obeying her' and says she feels unsteady on her feet constantly. Her urinary urgency began approximately 18 months ago, with three to four episodes of leakage per week, mainly with urgency or a delay in reaching the toilet; she wears protective underwear daily. Cognitive symptoms include increasing word-finding difficulty, misplacing objects, difficulty calculating change and repeating herself in conversation. She is an extremely detail-oriented person by training and is acutely aware of her deficits, which distresses her greatly. She denies headache, diplopia, tremor or numbness. There is no history of head injury, meningitis or intracranial hemorrhage. A head CT obtained by her internist three weeks ago was reported as showing enlarged ventricles; the images are not available. She was referred by her internist for progressive gait difficulty with memory decline and urinary urgency.

neurological_exam.additional: Bilateral grasp reflexes. No nuchal rigidity. No residual deformity or tenderness of the right wrist after the prior fall.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. No papilledema. PERRL. Horizontal and vertical gaze intact.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based, magnetic, short-stepped gait with reduced foot clearance. Freezing on initiation. Reduced arm swing. Cannot tandem walk. Pull test: 2 steps backward, recovers unaided. Walks with a cane.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, attentive, oriented to person, place and day. Mildly distressed by her deficits. Slowed responses. No aphasia. Formal cognitive screening reported separately.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal tone. No rigidity. No resting tremor. Mild hip flexor weakness bilaterally (4+/5); strength otherwise full.
neurological_exam.sensory: Normal to light touch and pinprick throughout. Vibration mildly reduced at ankles.
